issues.legal_issue: A transferee qualifies for the statutory protection for a purchaser only when the transfer is a bona fide purchase for consideration, established by reliable evidence.
material_facts: The property was purchased at a court auction by a person connected to the decree-holder’s family and was later assigned to two transferees, one of whom was related to the auction purchaser’s family.
The assignment deeds recited consideration, but the evidence supporting substantial parts of the stated consideration was contradictory or absent.
The appellate courts relied on tax, rent and revenue records and the parties’ assertions about payment, without adequately assessing the family relationships or the gaps in proof of consideration.
The Supreme Court found that the evidence and circumstances did not establish bona fide purchases for consideration.
issues.conclusion: The transferees were not bona fide purchasers for consideration and were not entitled to the protection of the proviso to Section 13(B)(1) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 13(B)(1) excludes restoration where the holding was sold to a bona fide purchaser for consideration within the specified statutory period. Whether a purchase is bona fide must be determined by evaluating the evidence and circumstances, including the relationship between the parties and whether the consideration recited in the transfer documents is substantiated. Tax, rent or revenue receipts alone do not dispel a competing claim. The Court relied on Section 13(B)(1).

rule.if: restoration_proceeding_case and related_transfer_parties and (consideration_evidence_unsupported or material_relationships_ignored)

predicates.restoration_proceeding_case: The case concerns a tenant’s application to set aside a sale and recover a holding under a statutory restoration scheme.
predicates.related_transfer_parties: The transferor and transferees had family or other close relationships relevant to evaluating the transaction.
predicates.consideration_evidence_unsupported: The evidence did not reliably substantiate material parts of the consideration recited in the transfer documents.
predicates.material_relationships_ignored: The fact-finders did not adequately consider relationships between the transaction participants when assessing the evidence.

issues.definition: When a restoration proceeding involves a related-party transfer and either the claimed consideration lacks reliable support or relevant relationships were ignored, the transferee is not treated as a bona fide purchaser.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere with concurrent factual findings when exceptional circumstances show that material evidence was ignored and the resulting decision caused manifest injustice or grave miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The appeal challenged concurrent appellate findings that the transferees were bona fide purchasers.
The appellate courts had overlooked or excluded material evidence, including relationships among the parties and the lack of reliable support for recitals of consideration.
The High Court did not address a substantial question concerning a relevant family relationship and disposed of the appeal on a short ground.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court was justified in exercising its discretionary jurisdiction to interfere with the concurrent findings and remedy the resulting injustice.
issues.legal_principle: Interference under Article 136 of the Constitution is sparing, but it is justified where exceptional circumstances show manifest injustice or grave miscarriage of justice caused by overlooking, ignoring or excluding material evidence. Once the burden of showing a manifestly unjust concurrent decision is discharged, the Court has a duty to remedy the injustice. The Court relied on Dipak Banerjee v. Lilabati Chakraborty, Basudev Hazra v. Meutiar Rahaman Mandal, and Bhanu Kumar Shastri v. Mohan Lal Sukhadia.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal_from_concurrent_fin: The proceeding is an appeal to the Supreme Court challenging concurrent factual findings by lower courts.
predicates.material_evidence_ignored: The lower courts overlooked, ignored or excluded evidence material to resolving the dispute.
predicates.resulting_manifest_injustice: The treatment of the evidence resulted in manifest injustice or a grave miscarriage of justice.

issues.definition: In an appeal from concurrent findings, ignored material evidence that results in manifest injustice permits the Supreme Court to interfere.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant is entitled to restoration under Section 13(B)(1) when the holding was sold in execution of a rent-arrears decree, the tenant was dispossessed within the statutory period, the statutory deposit and application requirements are met, and no qualifying bona fide purchase bars restoration.
material_facts: The holding was sold at a court auction in execution of a decree for arrears of rent.
The applicants were tenants and were dispossessed through delivery of the holding to the auction purchaser after the statutory commencement date and before the amending legislation came into force.
The tenants later trespassed onto the property and were ejected under a decree in a separate suit; that later event followed, and did not alter, their initial dispossession through the auction sale.
The tenants applied for restoration and had made the required deposit in an earlier restoration proceeding.
The transferees were not bona fide purchasers for consideration.
issues.conclusion: The tenants were entitled to restoration of possession; the later decree to recover possession from their trespass did not defeat that entitlement.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(B)(1) applies where a holding is sold in execution of a decree for arrears of rent and the tenant is dispossessed within the specified statutory period. The only bar identified in the subsection is a qualifying sale to a bona fide purchaser for consideration. The tenant must also make the required deposit and apply to the court for setting aside the sale and restoration. A later recovery of possession from a tenant who trespassed after the auction purchaser had obtained delivery does not change the fact or legal character of the original dispossession. The Court relied on Section 13(B)(1) and its proviso.

rule.if: tenant_restoration_proceeding and rent_arrears_execution_sale and covered_dispossession and deposit_and_application_made and not bona_fide_purchase_bar

predicates.tenant_restoration_proceeding: The proceeding is an application by a tenant to set aside a sale and recover the holding.
predicates.rent_arrears_execution_sale: The holding was sold in execution of a decree for arrears of rent.
predicates.covered_dispossession: The tenant was dispossessed during the period covered by the restoration scheme.
predicates.deposit_and_application_made: The tenant made the required deposit and applied to the court for setting aside the sale and restoring possession.
predicates.bona_fide_purchase_bar: The holding was sold to a bona fide purchaser for consideration in circumstances that trigger the statutory bar.

issues.definition: A tenant in a restoration proceeding is entitled to recover the holding when the sale and dispossession meet the scheme’s conditions, the deposit and application requirements are met, and no qualifying bona fide purchase bars restoration.

issues.legal_issue: A restoration application and deposit made under an earlier temporary enactment and still pending when that enactment is repealed may continue under the later enactment.
material_facts: The tenants filed a restoration application under an earlier temporary enactment and deposited the purchase money and interest required for that proceeding.
That application was pending when the earlier enactment was repealed and the later enactment came into force.
The tenants sought to have the earlier application and deposit treated as continuing in the later proceeding, and undertook to pay any deficiency found by the court.
The lower appellate court found the deposit sufficient, subject to deposit of any further interest if restoration was allowed; the High Court did not dislodge that finding.
issues.conclusion: The earlier pending application and deposit continued unaffected by the later enactment and could support the tenants’ claim for restoration.
issues.legal_principle: Whether repeal destroys rights or liabilities accrued under an earlier enactment depends on whether the later enactment manifests an intention to destroy them, not merely on whether it expressly preserves them. The Court approved the approach in Parameswaran Nambudiri’s case and relied on State of Punjab v. Mohar Singh. It also applied the requirements of Section 13(B) in the later enactment.

rule.if: restoration_proceeding_case and earlier_application_pending_at_repeal and required_deposit_already_made and no_intention_to_destroy_accrued_rights

predicates.restoration_proceeding_case: The proceeding concerns an application to restore a holding after a sale in execution for rent arrears.
predicates.earlier_application_pending_at_repeal: The tenant’s restoration application under the earlier enactment was still pending when that enactment was repealed.
predicates.required_deposit_already_made: The tenant had made the deposit required for the earlier restoration proceeding.
predicates.no_intention_to_destroy_accrued_rights: The later enactment did not manifest an intention to destroy rights and liabilities accrued under the earlier enactment.

issues.definition: A pending restoration application with the required deposit continues after repeal when the later enactment does not show an intention to destroy the accrued rights involved.
